title: What's new in product: February 2024
summary: Discover our latest product update, bringing you a suite of new AI tools to help you create even more stunning product photos - and faster.
body_text: This February, Photoroom is excited to announce a series of big product updates empowering higher image quality and creative control for our users. From our very own foundation model built for product photography, to a suite of AI tools and features by popular demand, we're cementing our position as the world’s most popular AI photo editor. But that's not all—more innovative features are on their way, so stay tuned for more updates! New Updates Curved Text You asked, and of course, we listened! Curved Text is available now on Photoroom. Previously known as Instant Backgrounds, our new AI Backgrounds allows you to create sharper, higher resolution, and more detailed backgrounds that look realistic and professional. For : Pro and Business users (beta) Platform : Photoroom for iOS Create anything with AI Images (beta) Forget about Midjourney, now you can use Photoroom to easily generate any AI images for marketing assets, inspo pictures, or for whatever you like! It’s available to a beta group of iOS users for initial feedback and will be available to all iOS users. ➡ Join the beta group here to get early access to this feature (iOS only). Coming soon in late spring to Android and the Web. title: 5 Best AI Visibility Tools for Startups
summary: Compare AI visibility tracking tools by total cost of ownership—monthly fees, setup labor, and consulting expenses. Find the best budget-friendly platform for startups monitoring ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude mentions.
body_text: When ChatGPT and Perplexity recommend vendors to your prospects, brands outside those AI-generated shortlists lose pipeline before the first sales call. Traditional analytics miss this layer of discovery entirely. For startups, the challenge isn't just tracking brand mentions—it's balancing subscription costs against setup labor and consulting fees to find tools that deliver actionable insights without breaking budgets. Key Takeaways Total cost of ownership—not monthly price—determines which AI visibility platform delivers startup value, combining subscription fees, setup labor, and consulting expenses Monitoring-only platforms ($25–$50/month) surface citation data but require $5,000–$15,000 in consulting fees to translate findings into optimization strategies Optimization-integrated tools bundle tracking with prescriptive guidance, eliminating downstream consulting dependency for resource-constrained teams Multi-engine coverage across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews prevents blind spots from platform-specific citation patterns Free validation tools work for baseline checks below 50 prompts per week but become operationally infeasible for ongoing competitive monitoring What 'Affordable' Actually Means for AI Visibility Tracking For startups on a tight budget, Siftly , Peec AI , and Profound represent optimization-integrated platforms that reduce total cost of ownership (TCO) by bundling monitoring, analysis, and prescriptive guidance into a single subscription, eliminating the consulting fees that turn low-priced monitoring-only tools into expensive dependencies. Why Monthly Price Alone Misleads Startups A $25/month monitoring-only platform that surfaces citation counts but offers no interpretation forces teams to hire consultants at $150, $250/hour to translate the data into actionable optimization steps. Over 12 months, a single 40-hour engagement ($6,000, $10,000) plus the subscription ($300) costs more than an $79/month optimization-integrated tool like Siftly's Starter plan that delivers automated recommendations alongside the metrics. Traditional analytics miss AI-generated brand mentions across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews, making dedicated visibility tracking key, but the hidden consulting dependency is where budget-conscious teams overspend. The Three TCO Components Competitors Hide Total cost of ownership breaks into three dimensions: (1) monthly subscription ($0, $499 for most mid-market platforms), (2) setup and integration labor (typically 10 to 40 hours of in-house time at $50, $150/hour for connecting data sources, configuring prompts, and training team members), and (3) ongoing consulting fees for interpretation and optimization work that monitoring-only tools don't provide. Platforms like Siftly bundle optimization recommendations directly into the dashboard, eliminating dimension three. Research shows AI visibility measurements require continuous tracking rather than one-time checks, rankings fluctuate across runs due to the probabilistic nature of generative models, meaning periodic manual snapshots miss critical shifts that automated platforms catch. The Siftly free tier monitors ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews with 30-day historical data, offering a zero-dollar entry point for validation before teams commit to paid automation. When Free Tiers Work (and When They Don't) Free validation tools, including Siftly's AI Visibility Checker , HubSpot's AEO Grader, and manual ChatGPT checks, serve as baseline-setting instruments for teams confirming whether their brand appears in AI responses before investing in ongoing monitoring. Manual tracking remains operationally feasible below 50 prompts per week and five competitors, but scaling beyond that threshold without automation leads to incomplete coverage and missed competitive intelligence. Because citation shares and rankings are snapshots of a continuously changing target rather than fixed facts, free one-time checks cannot replace the repeated measurements that distinguish genuine visibility shifts from statistical noise. Siftly's free plan bridges the validation-to-monitoring gap by delivering automated checks at no cost, though teams needing optimization recommendations or expanded platform coverage (Gemini, Perplexity, Claude) require the Starter tier at $79/month. Understanding the affordability framework sets the foundation for evaluating specific platform categories. The next step is distinguishing between monitoring-only dashboards and optimization-integrated systems, a choice that fundamentally reshapes total cost of ownership. Monitoring-Only Vs. Optimization-Integrated: the TCO Trade-Off Monthly subscription price is only one variable in the total cost equation. Monitoring-only platforms advertise entry prices as low as $25-50/month but deliver passive reporting, visibility scores, mention counts, competitor rankings, without prescriptive guidance on how to act on the data. Teams then hire separate consultants at $5,000 to $15,000 per project to interpret findings and build optimization roadmaps. That hidden consulting line item often eclipses the annual subscription cost within a single engagement. What Monitoring-Only Platforms Actually Deliver Monitoring-only platforms track brand mentions across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, and Claude, returning dashboards that show whether your brand appeared, how often, and which competitors ranked higher. They generate reports but stop short of prescriptive recommendations. If the data reveals that a competitor owns the top three prompts in your category, the platform flags the gap, but provides no guidance on which content to ship, which sources to pursue, or how to structure answers that LLMs prefer. That interpretation labor falls on your team, and most startups lack the in-house GEO expertise to translate visibility metrics into actionable tasks without external consulting support. How Optimization-Integrated Platforms Cut Downstream Labor Optimization-integrated platforms, like Siftly's Starter tier at $79/month, Peec AI, and Profound, bundle monitoring with prescriptive optimization recommendations. When the dashboard surfaces a visibility gap, the platform also delivers content gap analysis, citable source suggestions, and structural improvements (FAQ schema, list formatting, citation-dense intro paragraphs) that increase mention probability. The system points to the specific pages that need work and explains why LLMs currently favor competitor content over yours. That eliminates the separate consulting engagement required to turn raw visibility data into a prioritized optimization roadmap, collapsing the workflow from data → consultant → action into data → action. Calculating the 12-Month TCO Crossover Point Total cost of ownership (TCO) calculation reveals when higher monthly pricing delivers lower total spend. Here's the four-step methodology: Monthly subscription × 12 : Monitoring-only tool at $25/month = $300 annual; optimization-integrated tool at $79/month = $948 annual. Setup time × hourly rate : Initial configuration typically requires 4-6 hours regardless of platform; assume $75/hour blended rate = $300-450 setup cost for both. Consulting engagement fees : Monitoring-only platforms require separate consulting to translate data into optimization roadmaps at $5,000-15,000 per project; optimization-integrated platforms bundle this work into the subscription, adding $0 in external consulting fees. Total TCO sum : Monitoring-only TCO = $300 subscription + $450 setup + $10,000 consulting (mid-range) = $10,750. Optimization-integrated TCO = $948 subscription + $450 setup + $0 consulting = $1,398. The crossover point arrives immediately: even at the low end of the consulting range ($5,000), monitoring-only TCO reaches $5,750 versus $1,398 for optimization-integrated platforms. The $54/month price delta is dwarfed by the avoided consulting engagement. Startups with technical capability or in-house GEO expertise may extract value from monitoring-only tools by building their own optimization workflows; teams lacking that expertise pay the consulting premium or leave visibility data unactionable. With the TCO trade-off clarified, the following comparison examines specific platforms across both categories. Each tool's feature set, pricing structure, and coverage scope reveals where it fits in the monitoring-only versus optimization-integrated spectrum. Budget AI Visibility Tools Compared Traditional analytics miss the growing layer of AI-powered discovery shaping buyer research, when prospects ask ChatGPT or Perplexity for vendor shortlists, brands outside those answers lose pipeline before sales ever hears from the lead. Startups on tight budgets need visibility into which AI engines recommend their brand, how often, and against which competitors. The platforms below split into two categories: monitoring-only tools that track mentions without optimization guidance, and optimization-integrated platforms that include actionable recommendations to improve citation rates. Monitoring-Only Platforms: Otterly, SE Ranking Monitoring-only tools track brand mentions across AI engines but require separate consulting or internal expertise to act on the data. SE Ranking's AI Visibility Tracker offers a 14-day free trial and tracks Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT, and Gemini. OtterlyAI monitors six platforms (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot) and provides mention counts, competitive positioning, and sentiment analysis. These platforms answer "are we visible?" but leave "how do we improve?" to the user. Expect to invest in-house GEO expertise or agency consulting to translate visibility data into content strategy, adding hidden labor costs not reflected in the monthly subscription. Optimization-Integrated Platforms: Siftly, Peec AI, Profound Optimization-integrated platforms combine monitoring with prescriptive guidance, reducing downstream consulting spend. Siftly's Starter plan ($79/month) tracks ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Gemini, and Perplexity with built-in optimization recommendations, competitive benchmarking, and real-time monitoring, teams get actionable next steps (which pages to update, which competitor gaps to own) alongside share of voice metrics. Growth and Scale tiers expand coverage; Enterprise adds Claude and unlimited responses. Peec AI and Profound serve similar use cases with prompt analysis and multi-engine dashboards. Optimization-integrated tools deliver lower total cost of ownership for startups without dedicated GEO staff, the platform surfaces content gaps and citation opportunities, eliminating the need for separate consultants to interpret the data. Platform Coverage Gaps and Why They Matter Single-platform tools (ChatGPT-only trackers) leave blind spots because citation patterns differ across engines. Perplexity favors academic and news sources; Google AI Overviews weight E-E-A-T signals; Claude and ChatGPT respond to different content structures. A brand ranking well in ChatGPT answers may be invisible in Perplexity results for the same query category. Multi-platform monitoring surfaces these asymmetries, if competitors dominate Perplexity but you own ChatGPT mentions, that gap informs content strategy (publish more in outlets Perplexity trusts). Results vary by industry competition and content quality; no platform guarantees specific visibility outcomes. For complete coverage, prioritize tools tracking at least four major engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI, Gemini or Claude) to capture where your buyers actually research. Platform comparisons highlight capabilities, but choosing the right category depends on your team's operational context. Three specific conditions determine when monitoring-only platforms deliver value, and when they create hidden costs. When to Choose Monitoring-Only (and When to Skip It) Three Scenarios Where Monitoring-Only Suffices Monitoring-only platforms work well for startups in three specific conditions. First, when you already have in-house GEO expertise, someone on your team who understands how LLMs select sources and can translate visibility data into content strategy without consulting support. Second, when query volume stays below 50 prompts per week and you're tracking fewer than five competitors, manual analysis remains operationally feasible. Third, during validation-stage tracking before scaling: run a 30-day baseline to prove AI search drives pipeline before investing in optimization-enabled tools. When Monitoring-Only Creates False Economy Monitoring-only tools can create a false economy in three failure modes. Without in-house GEO expertise, raw visibility data requires $5,000 to 15,000 in consulting fees to interpret and act on, erasing the monthly subscription savings. When query volume exceeds 50 prompts per week or you're tracking more than five competitors, manual analysis becomes operationally infeasible and critical patterns get missed. In high-competitive-pressure environments, optimization cycles that depend on consulting introduce 2 to 4 week delays that cost market position. Platforms like Siftly bundle optimization recommendations with monitoring, eliminating the consulting dependency for teams without dedicated GEO resources. The Volume Threshold That Makes Automation Necessary Manual tracking hits an operational ceiling at 50 prompts per week and five competitors. Above that threshold, API-based platforms become necessary: a human can manually query and log 10 to 15 prompts per day, but tracking 50+ prompts across five competitors and four platforms (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Gemini) requires 200+ discrete queries weekly. At that scale, automation isn't a convenience, it's the only way to maintain consistent visibility measurement and catch trend shifts before they compound. Decision frameworks provide directional guidance, but calculating exact costs before committing prevents budget surprises. A structured TCO evaluation translates abstract platform features into concrete twelve-month expenditures. How to Evaluate Total Cost of Ownership Before You Buy AI visibility tracking platforms vary in subscription price, but the real cost includes setup labor, ongoing maintenance, and consulting fees for optimization. Use this four-step TCO calculation to compare tools accurately before committing budget. Step 1: Calculate Monthly Subscription × 12 Months Start with the base subscription cost. Most platforms gate prompt volumes by tier, free plans cap at 10 to 20 prompts per month, while Starter tiers unlock 50 to 100. Multiply your required tier's monthly rate by 12. For example, Siftly's Starter tier at $79/month yields $948 annually. Verify current rates on vendor pricing pages, pricing changes frequently. Step 2: Estimate Setup and Integration Labor Hours Monitoring-only platforms require API integration and dashboard configuration, budget 2 to 4 hours at your team's hourly rate ($100, $200/hour for mid-level marketers). Optimization-integrated platforms add onboarding calls and content audits, typically 4 to 8 hours total. Setup complexity scales with platform breadth: tools like Ahrefs demand steeper learning curves due to expansive feature sets, mirroring the technical expertise overhead in AI visibility tools. Multiply setup hours by your blended hourly rate to quantify this hidden cost. Step 3: Add Consulting Fees for Optimization Monitoring-only platforms deliver passive reporting, citation counts and share of voice, but leave optimization strategy to you. If your team lacks AI search expertise, expect $5,000, $15,000 in consulting fees to translate data into content fixes and citation outreach. Optimization-integrated platforms include prescriptive recommendations and automated content generation, eliminating this line item. For resource-constrained startups, this difference defines whether a tool fits budget. Step 4: Factor in Ongoing Maintenance Overhead After setup, account for recurring labor: manual report interpretation (1 to 2 hours weekly), competitive benchmarking updates (2 to 4 hours monthly), and optimization execution (4 to 8 hours monthly). Monitoring-only tools leave all execution to your team, roughly 10 to 15 hours per month at $150/hour = $1,500, $2,250 ongoing monthly cost. Optimization-enabled platforms automate much of this workflow, reducing maintenance to light review cycles. Worked example: Siftly Starter ($79/month × 12 = $948) + setup (4 hours × $150 = $600) + $0 consulting = $1,548 annual TCO . Compare to monitoring-only: ($25/month × 12 = $300) + setup (2 hours × $150 = $300) + consulting ($10,000) = $10,600 annual TCO . The $79/month tool costs 85% less over 12 months when labor and expertise gaps are included. Conclusion Monitoring-only platforms like Otterly and SE Ranking offer lower monthly subscriptions ($25, $50) but require separate consulting engagements ($5,000 to 15,000) to translate passive reporting into actionable optimization, higher total cost of ownership for startups without in-house GEO expertise. Optimization-integrated platforms like Siftly, Peec AI, and Profound have higher entry prices ($79, $150/month) but include prescriptive recommendations that eliminate consulting dependency, lower TCO for resource-constrained teams. As AI search adoption accelerates through 2026, visibility tracking will shift from nice-to-have monitoring to must-have attribution infrastructure, early adopters who baseline their visibility now will capture the citation equity that late entrants spend years chasing. Document your current AI citation baseline this week using Siftly's free visibility checker , then use the TCO framework from this guide to evaluate which platform category suits your query volume and in-house expertise. Above that threshold, free tools cap query volumes and exclude competitive benchmarking, making them unsuitable for ongoing monitoring. Multi-engine coverage prevents gaps in visibility intelligence. When should I choose a monitoring-only platform vs an optimization-integrated tool? Monitoring-only suffices if you have in-house GEO expertise, query volume below 50 prompts per week, and low competitive pressure. Above those thresholds or without internal expertise, optimization-integrated platforms deliver lower TCO by eliminating $5,000 to 15,000 in consulting fees that monitoring-only tools require for actionable recommendations. Can I use ChatGPT search to manually track brand mentions instead of paying for a tool? title: When AI Branding Goes Too Far: Over-Branded Training Video
summary: Learn how to prevent AI video over branding, protect instructional clarity, use semantic color accessibly, and review logos, motion, and templates.
body_text: A practical identity-versus-instruction framework Separate the visual system into four layers. Layer 1: Identity This includes the approved logo, type family, core palette, tone, and signature motifs. Use it to establish provenance and continuity. Opening and closing cards, section markers, and selected framing elements are natural locations. Layer 2: Navigation Progress markers, chapter labels, lower thirds, and repeated layouts help learners orient themselves. These can borrow brand styling, but they must remain readable and should not compete with the current step. Layer 3: Meaning Status, risk, category, comparison, sequence, and feedback belong here. Meaning takes priority over decorative uniformity. Pair color with text or shape, and document semantic rules. Layer 4: Content Screenshots, equipment, charts, people, and real environments should remain accurate. Do not recolor a product interface, safety sign, map, uniform, or real object just to match the palette if doing so reduces fidelity or changes meaning. When layers conflict, prioritize content accuracy, instructional meaning, accessibility, navigation, and then decoration. Knowlify’s complete guide to training videos starts from learning purpose rather than production effects. Its step-by-step training video guide also explains why one observable objective should govern what stays and what gets cut. Semantic color examples Example 1: Compliance knowledge check An organization’s primary brand color is red. The first design uses red for the selected answer, the submit button, section headings, and the incorrect state. That makes selection and error difficult to distinguish. A better system uses: brand red for identity framing and selected decorative emphasis a clear border plus “Selected” label for the chosen option an error icon, the word “Incorrect,” and an accessible error surface for wrong answers a check icon, the word “Correct,” and a separately tested success surface a neutral, high-contrast submit control The exact hues can remain compatible with the identity, but the states no longer depend on hue alone. Example 2: Safety procedure A brand palette contains yellow as an accent. The team wants to use yellow for every heading and transition. The safety procedure also uses yellow to mark caution. The solution is to reserve the recognized caution treatment for actual cautions and move decorative emphasis to another brand element, perhaps a navy line, shape, or typographic weight. This protects the meaning of yellow within the lesson. Example 3: Data chart A one-color chart technically looks branded, but its six series are hard to tell apart. Use a tested categorical palette and reinforce categories with direct labels, line styles, patterns, or symbols. Apply the brand through title treatment, typography, framing, and a selective highlight of the series that matters. Example 4: Logo on complex footage The full-color logo disappears over a moving background. Adding a large opaque box behind it throughout the video preserves recognition but obscures the demonstration. Better options include showing the logo on a clean opening and closing card, using an approved high-contrast variant in a safe area, or omitting the persistent watermark. W3C notes that logos are exempt from certain contrast requirements, but also recommends considering a sufficiently contrasting variant when a logo acts as a user interface component. The exemption does not make an unreadable mark useful. How to de-brand an overloaded video Use this review sequence on a representative draft. Pass 1: Remove repetition Temporarily hide every logo, slogan, border, corner shape, and branded transition. Add back only what establishes source or structure. Most teams discover that an opening mark, closing card, type system, and a few accents do enough. Pass 2: Restore hierarchy Choose one focal point per scene. Reduce saturation and motion in secondary elements. Ensure the title, demonstrated action, or key diagram, not the brand furniture, receives the strongest emphasis. Pass 3: Audit meaning List every color and what it communicates. If one color means “brand,” “selected,” “warning,” and “incorrect,” split those roles. If meaning is carried only by color, add words, icons, patterns, positions, or shapes. Pass 4: Test accessibility Check text contrast using actual frames, not only palette swatches. Text over video can pass on one frame and fail on the next; use a stable surface, overlay, outline, or different placement. Test important graphics and controls as well. Pass 5: Test without sound and at small size Turn off sound, enable captions, and view the video at the smallest expected player size. Confirm that captions are not blocked and that repeated branding does not consume the readable area. Pass 6: Ask learners Show the revised video to representative users. Ask what they noticed first, what the colors meant, and what action they would take. Do not ask only whether it “looks on-brand.” Teams producing many modules can pair this review with the governance practices in Knowlify’s article on microlearning video at enterprise scale . A pre-publication over-branding checklist The learning objective is visible in the content, not buried under an identity sequence. Logos appear at a defined cadence and never obscure demonstrations or captions. Each scene has one clear focal point. Brand accents are selective enough to retain emphasis. Functional colors have documented meanings. Color is never the only cue for status, feedback, category, or required action. Normal and large text meet the chosen WCAG contrast target. Charts and diagrams remain distinguishable in greyscale and for users with color-vision differences. Real products, interfaces, controls, and safety markings are not misleadingly recolored. Motion and sound branding are brief and not repeatedly distracting. The design works in every intended aspect ratio and player size. An accessibility or learning reviewer can override brand usage with a recorded reason. FAQ How often should a logo appear in a training video? There is no universal count. An opening card, closing card, and occasional unobtrusive identifier may be enough. Frequency should reflect distribution risk and brand policy without competing with the lesson. Are logos exempt from WCAG contrast rules? Text that is part of a logo or brand name is exempt from WCAG 2.2’s text contrast requirement. That narrow exception does not cover ordinary branded text, diagrams, controls, or the rest of the corporate palette. Can brand colors be used for correct and incorrect feedback? Yes, if the colors are distinguishable, meet applicable contrast needs, and are reinforced with non-color cues such as “Correct” and “Incorrect,” icons, shapes, or patterns. Does a less branded video look unprofessional? Not necessarily. Consistent typography, composition, voice, pacing, and a restrained identity frame often feel more deliberate than constant logo and color repetition. Who should approve exceptions to brand guidelines? Define this in advance. Typically the brand owner is consulted, while accessibility, legal, safety, or instructional requirements can justify a documented exception. title: Dave Announces Pricing of $175 Million 0% Convertible Notes
body_text: Company entered into capped call transactions to increase effective conversion premium to 100% Company to repurchase approximately 334,000 shares of common stock using approximately $70.5 million of net proceeds Los Angeles, March 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Dave Inc. (Nasdaq: DAVE) (“Dave” or the “Company”) today announced the pricing of an offering of $175 million principal amount of its 0% Convertible Senior Notes due 2031 (the “notes”) through a private offering to persons reasonably believed to be qualified institutional buyers pursuant to Rule 144A under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”). Dave has also granted the initial purchasers an option to purchase, for settlement within a 13-day period beginning on, and including, the date Dave first issues the notes, up to an additional $25 million principal amount of notes. The offering was upsized from the previously announced offering of $150 million principal amount. The offering is expected to close on March 9, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. The notes will be senior unsecured obligations of Dave. The notes will not bear regular interest, and the principal amount of the notes will not accrete. The notes will mature on April 1, 2031, unless earlier converted, redeemed or repurchased. Dave may redeem for cash all or any portion of the notes (subject to a partial redemption limitation), at Dave’s option, on or after April 6, 2029 and prior to the 41st scheduled trading day immediately preceding the maturity date, only if (i) certain liquidity conditions are met and (ii) the last reported sale price of Dave’s Class A common stock (the “common stock”) has been at least 130% of the conversion price then in effect for at least 20 trading days (whether or not consecutive), including the trading day immediately preceding the date on which Dave provides notice of redemption, during any 30 consecutive trading day period ending on, and including, the trading day immediately preceding the date on which Dave provides the related notice of redemption at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the notes to be redeemed, plus accrued and unpaid special interest, if any, up to, but excluding, the redemption date. Prior to the close of business on the business day immediately preceding January 1, 2031, the notes will be convertible at the option of the holders only upon the satisfaction of certain conditions and during certain periods. Dave estimates that the net proceeds from the offering will be approximately $168.0 million (or approximately $192.1 million if the initial purchasers exercise in full their option to purchase additional notes), after deducting initial purchasers’ discounts and estimated offering expenses. Dave intends to use the net proceeds from the offering (i) to fund the approximate $15.1 million cost of the capped call transactions described below, (ii) to repurchase approximately 334,000 shares of common stock, using approximately $70.5 million of the net proceeds from the offering as described below and (iii) for general corporate purposes, including additional share repurchases under our share repurchase program. In connection with the pricing of the notes, Dave has entered into privately negotiated capped call transactions with one or more of the initial purchasers of the notes or their respective affiliates and other financial institutions (the “capped call counterparties”). The capped call transactions cover, subject to anti-dilution adjustments substantially similar to those applicable to the notes, the number of shares of common stock that initially underlie the notes, assuming the initial purchasers do not exercise their option to purchase additional notes. The cap price of the capped call transactions is initially $421.34 per share of common stock, representing a premium of 100% above the last reported sale price of $210.67 per share of common stock on March 4, 2026, and is subject to certain adjustments under the terms of the capped call transactions. The capped call transactions are expected generally to reduce potential dilution to the common stock upon conversion of the notes and/or offset any cash payments that Dave could be required to make in excess of the principal amount of any converted notes upon conversion thereof, as the case may be, with such reduction and/or offset subject to a cap. If the initial purchasers exercise their option to purchase additional notes, Dave expects to enter into additional capped call transactions with the capped call counterparties. In connection with establishing their initial hedges of the capped call transactions, the capped call counterparties have advised Dave that they or their respective affiliates expect to enter into various derivative transactions with respect to the common stock concurrently with, or shortly after, the pricing of the notes, and they may unwind these various derivative transactions and purchase common stock in open market transactions shortly after the pricing of the notes. This activity could increase (or reduce the size of any decrease in) the market price of the common stock or the notes at that time. In addition, the capped call counterparties or their respective affiliates may modify their hedge positions by entering into or unwinding various derivatives with respect to the common stock and/or purchasing or selling the common stock or other of Dave’s securities in secondary market transactions following the pricing of the notes and prior to the maturity of the notes (and are likely to do so (x) during any observation period related to a conversion of the notes on or after January 1, 2031, (y) during any observation period related to a conversion of the notes prior to January 1, 2031 or following any repurchase of the notes by Dave on any fundamental change repurchase date, any redemption date or any other date on which Dave retires any notes, in each case, if Dave elects to terminate the relevant portion of the capped call transactions, and (z) in connection with any negotiated unwind or modification of the capped call transactions). This activity could also cause or avoid an increase or a decrease in the market price of the common stock or the notes, which could affect noteholders’ ability to convert the notes and, to the extent the activity occurs during any observation period related to a conversion of the notes, it could affect the number of shares, if any, and value and/or amount of the consideration that noteholders will receive upon conversion of the notes. Concurrently with the pricing of the offering, Dave has agreed to repurchase approximately 334,000 shares of common stock from purchasers of notes in privately negotiated transactions effected with or through one of the initial purchasers or its affiliate, at a purchase price per share equal to the last reported sale price of $210.67 per share of the common stock on March 4, 2026. body_text: Ask a naive agent to find a bug in a codebase with thousands of repositories, and it will find the first textual match and stop. It won't ask why. It won't check whether what it found is actually relevant. It won't explore related services. It'll just return something and call it done. We, at Wix , discovered this the hard way. And it's what pushed us to build something more deliberate: a research engine that doesn't just search, but reasons about what it's looking for and why. The Problem: Search Doesn't Scale to Org Complexity At Wix, finding anything specific inside the codebase is genuinely challenging. Thousands of services, thousands of developers, every team with their own agents and tooling, all of them pushing code continuously. When a bug surfaces in production, the question isn't just "where is the relevant code" it's "which of the thirty services that touch this feature is actually responsible, what was the database state at the time, what do the logs say happened, and is this behavior even a bug or is it by design?" A year ago, someone asked me to find a specific link somewhere in our system. I spent two days on GitHub. That experience stuck with me. Not because finding things is inherently hard, but because the tooling we had wasn't built for the kind of cross-service, cross-context search that makes up a huge chunk of daily engineering work. When we started building Wix Octocode Orchestrator, our autonomous bug-fixing system and needed an enrichment layer to gather context before attempting any fix, I had a clear picture of what not to build: a wrapper around GitHub search that just returns the first match. What We Built: OctoCode, and Then Wix Octocode Research I started by building OctoCode initially for myself, as an MCP server on top of GitHub's tooling. The goal was simple: help agents navigate repositories intelligently, understand relationships between packages and services, and get real definitions of things instead of textual guesses. Eleven months later, OctoCode sits at around 90,000 downloads , 5,000 weekly active users , and 4,500 weekly downloads . That adoption wasn't the plan it came from solving a real problem that turns out to be universal in any large engineering organization. What made it different from raw GitHub search was a set of deliberate design decisions around how agents use tools: Every tool call requires a stated reason. Before calling any tool, the agent must articulate its research goal and why it's making this specific call. This isn't bureaucratic overhead, it forces the agent to actually think about what it's looking for rather than pattern-matching on surface-level keywords. The reasoning becomes part of the context window, which means subsequent calls benefit from what was already figured out. Parallel branch exploration. Instead of a linear search, find one thing, decide, move on, agents can explore multiple branches simultaneously. Check the service that's most likely responsible and the service that's adjacent and the documentation that describes expected behavior, all at once. This dramatically reduces the time to a complete picture. Semantic fallback hints. When a search returns nothing useful, instead of giving up, the agent receives a hint: try searching for something semantically similar to what you were looking for. No vector database required just a prompt-level instruction that tells the agent to broaden its search strategy. Hints on tool responses. When a tool returns results, it also returns guidance on what to do next. This keeps the agent from getting stuck or looping, and means the search process is guided by accumulated context rather than starting fresh with each call. All of this came from failure, not design. Every one of these mechanisms exists because I watched something break and figured out why. Wix Octocode Research: Plugging OctoCode Into the Wix Octocode Orchestrator Pipeline OctoCode solves the GitHub search problem. Wix Octocode Research, the enrichment service that powers Wix Octocode Orchestrator solves the wider problem: assembling complete context across everything relevant to a bug, not just code. Wix Octocode Research uses OctoCode for static code analysis, Trino for normalized query access across all Wix databases, Grafana for live logs and runtime errors, and our internal and public documentation to determine whether a behavior is a bug or by design. Its output isn't just data, it's a structured research plan that the coding agent downstream can act on directly. Under the hood, Wix Octocode Research's architecture has three layers: 1. The Planner takes the incoming research request, a support ticket, a Jira issue, a bug description and unpacks it. It identifies the intent, determines what the output schema should look like (because different downstream services want answers in different formats), does an initial documentation pass, and queries memory for anything relevant we've already learned. Only then does it hand off to the Researcher. 2. The Researcher is a full orchestrator with access to all of our tooling OctoCode, Trino, Grafana, documentation, and a set of sub-agents. Those sub-agents are the key architectural decision: rather than one agent with fifty tools crammed into its context window, we have specialized agents: a database agent, a logs agent, a code agent each with a focused toolset and their own MCP server. Why? Because a database agent whose entire context is about querying and interpreting database results is far more effective than a general agent juggling everything at once. Context windows are finite, and attention matters. The cost is complexity at the boundary getting the schema right for how sub-agents return context back to the orchestrator took significant iteration, and we're still refining it. We also experimented with dynamic helpers : instead of calling a fixed set of sub-agents, the orchestrator can spin up an ad-hoc agent with exactly the tools needed for a specific investigation. A query that needs Grafana plus code analysis plus a database lookup gets one agent with those three tools, rather than three round-trips through separate sub-agents. The tradeoff between flexibility and predictability is still something we're working through. 3. The Memory Layer is what makes the system learn. Every completed research cycle the query, the planning decisions, the tools called, and the final output gets embedded and stored in a vector database. On the next similar request, the Planner retrieves those embeddings as hints, giving the Researcher a head start. Beyond storing results, the system also reviews itself: after each research cycle, the orchestrator reflects on which tools worked well, which instructions were effective, and feeds that back into the process. A Design Principle That Took Us Too Long to Learn When we first built Wix Octocode Research, the architecture was: Researcher does the work, hands off to a separate formatting agent to produce the final output. Seemed clean. It failed. The formatting agent had no understanding of what the Researcher had actually discovered. It produced generic, shallow responses because it had no context for why anything mattered. The lesson: the agent that does the hard investigative work should be the one that produces the output. Fighting the Frameworks: Why We Forked Google's ADK When designing Wix Octocode Research’s orchestration layer, we evaluated existing frameworks. LangChain felt too unstable for production breaking changes across frequent version updates made it hard to rely on at our scale. We moved to Google's ADK, which had a strong vendor behind it and a cleaner model. But building at scale always comes with a tax. The ADK's documentation and examples were written for Python, and we were deep into a TypeScript effort. That meant forking the framework and doing significant heavy lifting ourselves. The bigger issue: out of the box, the TypeScript ADK executed MCP tool calls sequentially one after another. For a research engine built entirely around parallel execution across GitHub, Trino, and Grafana, sequential calls were a performance killer. We rewrote the core tool-calling mechanism to support true concurrency, and optimized the token compaction logic ourselves. More maintainability debt, but the customizability we needed. A second principle that saved us significant debugging time: uniform tool protocols. Every tool in Wix Octocode Research regardless of what it queries speaks the same language: before calling, state why; when returning, include hints about what to do next. When agents share a protocol, the math of attention works in your favor. Agents don't have to spend context figuring out how each tool works they already know. What's Still Hard Finding specific records in a database from a high-level bug description is genuinely difficult. Isolating the right error from Grafana across dozens of services producing logs simultaneously is genuinely difficult. We haven't solved these, we're actively working on improving both, and we're honest about the gap between what the system can do today and what we need it to do. The organizational knowledge problem is also unsolved. Teams have context that lives in Slack threads and people's heads, which services are in the middle of a migration, which behaviors are intentional despite looking broken, which architectural constraints make an otherwise-obvious fix dangerous. We're building toward a model where each team maintains their own knowledge agent, and Wix Octocode Research can query those agents as part of any research cycle, without forcing teams into a specific format or tooling choice. To tackle this structural knowledge gap, we're developing CDD Context Driven Development . The idea is to give every engineering unit at Wix a simple interface to explicitly declare their domain context: their active repositories, primary database tables, and external dependencies. By making context declaration a first-class part of the development lifecycle, we can feed structured, up-to-date data directly into Wix Octocode Research's Planner, moving away from guessing toward precise architectural alignment. Conclusion: The Centrality of Learning and Measurement at Scale The long-term success of any self-healing system at an organization's scale fundamentally relies on constant measurement and moving from static processes to a continuous feedback and learning loop. For systems like Wix Octocode Research, this iterative process is baked into the architecture: Closed-Loop Learning: The system must operate as a closed control loop. Wix Octocode Research’s Memory Layer stores embeddings of every completed research cycle, including planning decisions and tool outcomes in a vector database. This gives the Planner a head start on similar requests by retrieving past resolutions as hints. Crucially, the orchestrator reflects on which tools were effective and feeds that learning back, ensuring continuous improvement and policy synthesis to reduce recurrence of similar defect classes. Key and Constant Measurement: Efficacy and accountability are enforced through a uniform tool protocol across all agents. This requires every tool call to state its reason and every return to include hints on the next steps. This protocol ensures the agent is reasoning and not pattern-matching, turning internal behavior into a measurable, traceable process. Structural Context Alignment (CDD): Overcoming the organizational knowledge problem requires a structural solution. Context Driven Development (CDD) mandates that every engineering unit explicitly declares their domain context (repositories, database tables, dependencies). By making this context declaration a first-class part of the development lifecycle, up-to-date data is fed directly into Wix Octocode Research’s Planner, moving the system toward precise architectural alignment rather than relying on guesswork. This emphasis on structural context, traceable protocol, and embedded outcome-driven learning is the core principle for building a research engine that doesn't just search, but reasons at massive scale. https://octocode.ai/ | Disclaimer: We are currently in ongoing improvements and learning cycles, constantly striving to optimize cost and quality while learning from every outcome. title: Safety mistakes ADT pros notice every summer — and what homeowners often miss
summary: ADT professionals with years of experience weigh in on the safety mistake patterns they see repeated that create risks.
body_text: With all the comings and goings during the summer, it can be easy to forget to set your alarm. An ADT Keypad near each entry helps make it easier to remember. The homeowner was in the shower when someone attempted to break in. Not from the front door, not from the back door, but from a window above a slanted roof — the kind most people assume no one can reach. The moment the window cracked open, the alarm went off, and the intruder ran away. Just weeks earlier, an ADT salesperson had convinced the homeowners to secure that exact window with an ADT Door/Window Sensor for added peace of mind, according to Aaron Light, ADT’s Virtual Installation Manager. ADT field professionals with years of experience in monitoring, installation, and sales say moments like this don’t come out of nowhere. Every summer, they see patterns repeat — not dramatic mistakes, but small, everyday decisions that quietly create risk. The good news is that most of what they see is preventable. Here’s how. Don’t spill the vacation tea Posting vacation plans in real time, tagging locations and sharing “we’re gone for a week” updates on social media — paired with abandoned packages and an overflowing mailbox — makes it easy to spot an empty home. Do this instead: Pause deliveries and clear the signs of an empty home, such as packages on the porch or a lawn that hasn’t been touched in days. Post your pics to social media after you’re home, not while you’re away. “The biggest red flag I see is people broadcasting their vacations on Facebook,” Light said. “Wait until you come back to share the photos and videos — don’t tell the world you’re away.” Use ADT+ Security System automations and smart devices, such as the ADT Dimming Lamp Module and ADT Smart Light Bulb , to schedule lighting that makes your home look occupied. And don’t forget to arm your system when you leave. “Customers sometimes tell me, ‘We live in a safe area, so I don’t really arm the system.’ That scares me,” said Steven Headley, an ADT HOA Account Manager. A smart doorbell connected to the ADT+ Security System lets you keep an eye on deliveries, even when you're away from home. Don’t forget about open doors and windows Kids are on break, going in and out of the house all day. People are letting in fresh air. This can lead to doors, windows and garages being left open or unarmed, ADT pros say. Increased use can also cause sensors to shift or prevent entry points from fully sealing. Do this instead: Confirm all doors and windows are fully closed so ADT Premium Door/Window Sensors are aligned, including garage doors, sliders and secondary entry points. “I’ve had customers call and say they can’t get their system to arm, and through troubleshooting, they find a window open or a door ajar in a room they don’t often use,” Headley said. “It only takes one person up to no good to see that from a distance.” Add ADT Glass Break Sensors to help detect forced entry if window glass is shattered rather than forced open. Look for windows that may be accessible, even above ground level. “I always encourage customers to put sensors on windows that are accessible from the ground — but people also overlook windows near slanted roofs,” Light said. “They think no one can get up there, but those windows can be accessible.” Don't let your landscaping obscure cameras Plants can grow quickly in summer, blocking sightlines and cameras. Additionally, ADT pros note that limited visibility and dark, hard-to-see areas around entry points can allow someone to test doors and windows without being noticed. Do this instead: Trim back landscaping so doors, windows and walkways are fully visible and cameras are not obscured. “I’ve seen branches hit cameras during storms, so cleaning up branches around the house is probably one of the best ways to prevent weather-related problems,” said Sean Miller, ADT Field Technician. Consider the Google Nest Cam with floodlight ,installed by an ADT professional, to help eliminate dark areas by triggering motion-activated lighting while capturing clear video of anyone lurking at night. Or, if you choose our ADT Blu DIY Outdoor Cameras make sure to position them so they have a clear, unobstructed line of sight to entry points and place them at a height that captures faces and movement, not just the top of someone’s head. Protect outdoor cameras during exterior home maintenance work to prevent damage. “I've seen multiple times where customers had their siding power-washed, and it caused their outdoor cameras to flood out,” said John Young, an Existing Customer Manager at ADT. Don’t inadvertently make a break-in easier Ladders, spare tools, stacked patio furniture and loose bricks can all give someone up to no good easier access to your home, ADT pros say. Do this instead: Lock up ladders, yard tools and any movable outdoor items that could be climbed on or used to force entry before you leave your home. “Don’t leave ladders out. Don’t leave anything somebody can use to break in — loose bricks, anything they could use to physically get into your home,” said Maurice Caples, ADT Existing Customer Technician. Keep sheds, pool houses, outdoor storage closets and garages protected by using ADT Blu Motion Sensors. “The biggest thing with garage sensors is cleaning around them. Get the debris away — cobwebs, even splash from a car can build up in that area affecting the sensors,” said Myles Cunningham, an ADT Customer Service Associate. Don't miss out on summer fun, worrying about safety. With ADT+, you can set automations to help run your security system. Don't forget to arm your system In summer, systems can go unused during the day because people are coming and going, or automations get turned off and never turned back on. ADT pros say this can lead to long stretches when homes aren’t actively protected. Do this instead: Use the ADT+ app to set up auto-arm and scheduled routines, and double-check that those automations are active. “With newer systems, you can actually have it auto-arm at certain times,” Miller said. Make sure everyone in your household knows how to arm, disarm and use the correct mode so the system isn’t left off or set incorrectly. Call ADT if you need help or reminders. “Sometimes it’s fear of not knowing how to use the system. Some customers are scared they’re going to have false alarms and have the police show up or the fire department,” Miller said. Verify all zones in your ADT system before arming, and resolve any alerts or bypassed sensors rather than ignoring them. “Sometimes people push off dealing with a concern, and then there’s an issue like a break-in, and they meant to call about that door sensor. If there is a problem, fix it,” Cunningham said. Don't forget to do regular system checks ADT pros say many households don’t test their systems regularly to confirm that alarms are triggering, signals are reaching our monitoring team, and the internet connection is strong. Dead batteries can make things worse, taking devices offline and creating coverage gaps. Do this instead: Check communication before you leave town and after storms, outages, home renovations or Wi-Fi changes. “Before you leave town, do one quick communication test while you’re still home,” said Ryan Mihalik, ADT Monitoring Unit Manager. “And renovations, storms, or lightning can impact the system, so when things come back up, you definitely want to test it and make sure it’s still communicating to us.” Inspect and clean sensors regularly, especially on less-used doors, windows and in garages or basements, and make sure sensor magnets are aligned, well-attached and able to register with your system. Place ADT Water and Temperature Sensors next to sump pumps and HVAC units to help detect leaks that can lead to widespread damage. Treat low-battery alerts, error messages and communication warnings as action items, not something to clear or bypass. “If there is a communication issue, it will say on the display: communication issue. Don’t wait, don’t hesitate — have a technician come in and check out the system.” Young said. Don’t put your health at risk from fire or CO2 Without professional monitoring, smoke and carbon monoxide alerts can go unnoticed when no one is home, putting pets and property at risk. ADT pros also notice that risks can build up in plain sight, with clutter near heat sources or equipment charging in poorly ventilated areas. And travel and busy summer schedules can lead to warning signs being ignored. Do this instead: Use professionally monitored ADT Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors so alerts can reach beyond the walls of your home. Cody Ellis, an ADT Service Technician, said the risk with standalone detectors is simple: “Nobody can hear it outside. Nobody knows anything about it.” Make sure those detectors are working. “Some people completely remove smoke detectors instead of fixing them when they chirp. It’s chirping at you for a reason. Change the battery or change the unit itself,” Caples said. Avoid charging large batteries, like those in golf carts, in poorly ventilated spaces. “The longer those batteries charge, the more gas certain types of batteries can release. If there’s no ventilation, that can be deadly,” Headley said. Avoid overloading a single outlet or power source with multiple devices, as this can cause overheating and increase fire risk. “Sometimes people have too much plugged into one outlet — fans, window air conditioners and other devices — and that can overheat the outlet, cause smoke, set off fire alarms or even cause fires,” said Letitia Oliver, an ADT Monitoring Manager. Above all, don’t get overwhelmed An ADT security system is meant to provide you with peace of mind, so you can relax and fully enjoy the summer season. If it starts to feel overwhelming, know that your system is backed by experienced professionals ready to help. Do this instead: “If you know you’re going away for a week, it doesn’t hurt to have us visit three weeks out and go over the system,” Young said. “Think of it like a car. If you maintain your system and invest a little bit of time into it, your system will last. It’s giving that little bit of extra tender loving care to it so you know everything will be good.” About the author Farah Saafan ADT Senior Writer #ADT experts #Our Employees #Safety trends

title: Introducing Apoxy Services
summary: Apoxy Services puts a JavaScript/Wasm runtime in your gateway. Write a fetch handler, deploy it with one command, and run it anywhere your gateway runs.
body_text: Today we're launching Apoxy Services, with workerd as the first runtime. Write a fetch handler against the workerd APIs, ship it to your Apoxy proxies or to the Cloudflare Workers® platform. API authentication handlers, response shaping, geo-aware logic, an experiment splitter, a thin shim that joins two services — anything you'd normally hand to a small backend service can run as an Apoxy Service instead. No new process to babysit, no separate cluster, no extra hop for your traffic to take. Why we built this There's a class of routing and policy decisions that belongs in front of your backend services. The conventional answer is to keep adding to the gateway's config language until it can express what you need. We prefer a different path. Apoxy Services puts a battle tested runtime in the gateway, so you can write code instead of config. It can handle the obvious gateway work: auth, rewrites, routing shaped by your tenancy model. But it doesn't stop there. You can ship a complete backend service with nothing else to run. Write a fetch handler An Apoxy Service is just a standard fetch handler: $ terminal TS export default { async fetch (request : Request ) : Promise < Response > { const url = new URL (request.url); if (url.pathname === "/health" ) { return Response. json ({ status: "ok" }); } const upstream = await fetch ( "https://api.example.com/data" ); return Response. json ( await upstream. json ()); } }; fetch() , Request , Response , Headers are all the same web APIs you'd write against in a browser or any web-standards runtime. Nothing proprietary, nothing you'll have to rewrite if you want to move it. One command to deploy If you wrote a fetch handler, you've already done the hard part. Now just deploy it — no registry to set up, no service.yaml to write first: $ terminal SH $ apoxy deploy --yes Deploying to project "acme" (production) ✓ name swift-hopper (generated; override with --name ) ✓ service.yaml wrote service.yaml ✓ build 1 module ( s ) → .apoxy/build ✓ push registry.apoxy.dev/ < project-i d > /swift-hopper@sha256:c9d2… ✓ apply Service/swift-hopper (digest sha256:c9d2… ) apoxy deploy builds your code into an OCI artifact and pushes it to your project's hosted private registry. On a first deploy it writes a minimal service.yaml for you, pins the pushed bundle digest into it, and applies the Service. The resulting artifact is immutable from the moment the build finishes. Bringing your own registry still works: set spec.source.oci.repo in service.yaml , or pass --repo , and apoxy deploy pushes there instead. Wire it to a route An Apoxy Service is simply another backend that any HTTPRoute can point at it: $ terminal YAML apiVersion : compute.apoxy.dev/v1alpha1 kind : Service metadata : name : hello-world spec : source : oci : repo : docker.io/yourorg/hello-world digest : sha256:c9d2… # pinned by `apoxy deploy` --- apiVersion : gateway.apoxy.dev/v1 kind : HTTPRoute metadata : name : api spec : parentRefs : - name : default kind : Gateway rules : - matches : - path : type : PathPrefix value : /api/ backendRefs : - group : compute.apoxy.dev kind : Service name : hello-world Run anywhere your gateway runs Most platforms that let you deploy edge logic put it on their infrastructure. Your function runs on their POPs, billed at their rate, or it doesn't run easily. Apoxy Services run on the Apoxy platform, where ever you deploy it. If your traffic is on our self-serve cloud, deploying a service will run it on our managed edge. To run a service inside your own cluster, you can deploy the gateway in your own cluster — which means either self-hosting using our open-source repo , or working with us to deploy and operate it in your VPC or colo with our team on-call 24/7. What's inside Apoxy Services is powered by workerd , the open-source JavaScript and Wasm runtime behind the Cloudflare Workers® platform. workerd is Apache 2.0 and we run it as-is. Each of your Services runs as its own V8 isolate inside a workerd process dedicated to your project, wrapped in our gVisor sandbox. We package workerd. We don't extend it, fork it, or rebrand its APIs. This means that upstream improvements ship to you when they ship to workerd with the same date-based compatibility guarantees. What it doesn't do yet Apoxy Services is in a public beta as of today's v0.21.0 release. There's a few things you need to know before pointing your production traffic at it: Tunnel upstreams are coming soon. We know that being able to dynamically route to upstreams connected via Tunnels is the dream, so we're working on it! No durable storage yet. You can call out to your databases and other services over fetch , but we do not have any built-in support for key-value stores or queues at this time. Secrets — API keys and other credentials — are supported today; see Secrets . Adjustable limits. We've limited execution time to 25ms for now, but if you need more time please let us know. Logs are basic. You'll get a simple per-request log today. Structured tracing across service → upstream and detailed per-execution logs are coming soon. If any of those are something you need right now then let us know and we'll try to get you early access. Get started Apoxy Services is available today on our self-serve plans. Check out the quickstart to get your first service deployed in about ten minutes. Try it out for free to start. No sales call required.
